arXiv:2611.21804v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.
title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies

arXiv:2611.21823v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.
title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark

arXiv:2611.22009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.
title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making

arXiv:2611.22085v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.
title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.22103v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.
title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution

0.24.0 (2026-10-15)

Key Changes

0.24.0 adds run-wide function error formatting and MCP discovery annotations, and improves recovery, sandbox safety, and tracing. This minor release includes compatibility changes for custom error callbacks and some saved agent graphs. Review the first two highlights before upgrading.

Highlights:

  • Update custom error formatters. RunConfig.tool_error_formatter can receive kind="tool_exception" and an optional error. Handle the new kind or return None to retain the default message. Explicit per-tool handlers keep precedence; unconfigured defaults stay unchanged.
  • Plan upgrades around saved runs. New RunState snapshots use schema 1.21. Finish affected older same-name agent graphs on their original SDK. Keep the agent code and original hook ordering unchanged. Use unique agent names for new durable runs; renaming a saved graph is not a migration.
  • Recover completed work more reliably. Deferred approval history, completed tool outputs, aliases, and compaction state survive supported recovery paths. Automatic compaction waits for approvals. Redis replaces history atomically on supported standalone clients. Conversations appends respect the 20-item request limit. Reconcile partial writes before retrying.
  • Harden local execution and display. macOS sandbox commands deny Launch Services requests. Sandbox tools recover from invalid model arguments. Protected mount errors preserve caller exception data while detaching the caught traceback. The realtime demo displays tool content as text.
  • Honor tracing choices through resume and cleanup. Per-run tracing opt-out applies inside caller traces, and approved resumed tools attach to the resumed agent span.
  • Use richer integration examples and metadata. MCP tools expose optional mcp_annotations as discovery hints. New Decisions recipes demonstrate classification, routing, and tool review with OpenAI >=3.26.0,<4. They use a separate client, not an Agents model adapter.
  • Refresh optional dependency locks. The Temporal extra uses temporalio==1.34.0; the Vercel extra supports vercel-sandbox>=0.7.0,<0.9. Core Python and OpenAI SDK minimums are unchanged.

Release call

🟢 GREEN LIGHT TO SHIP. The prepared 0.24.0 candidate has no unresolved release blocker. Its compatibility changes have supported migration or fallback paths described below.

Scope summary

  1. Route affected saved runs to their original SDK and agent code.

The reader rejects certain older graphs with same-name non-root agents whose saved identity ordering could have depended on hook attributes, even when those attributes remained unchanged.     • Risk: 🟢 LOW, with an explicit migration for exhaustive callbacks. A formatter that treats every non-rejection as a missing tool can now return misleading text for a crashed function.
    • Evidence: ToolErrorFormatterArgs.kind adds "tool_exception"; the optional error field is appended. The run-wide callback now handles eligible decorated function failures. For client-managed runs, accepted call/output pairs survive sibling or callback failures after input and tool-output guardrails permit publication. raw_summary:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.

In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.

Reviewing code is hard

Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.

To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:

  1. LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.
  2. LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.
  3. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes.

How Sashiko reviews a patch

To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:

Notes on each step:

  1. Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.

  2. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.

  3. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.

  4. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.

  5. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.

All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.

What the data shows

The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.

It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle.

It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization.

Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic.

Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%.

A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). 

That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch.

This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch:

"As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds (on lore.kernel.org)

What we learned from building and running Sashiko

First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level).

Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced.

Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning, Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers.

More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration.

Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git.

"Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML

You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev, or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.
source: Google Cloud AI and Machine Learning Blog

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.21998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.
title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.22030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.
title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition

raw_summary:
Software development is moving from individual agents completing tasks to teams of agents working on more complex projects.

A single agent can track its work in a Markdown file, but there isn't a purpose-built primitive for tracking tasks, delegation, statuses, logs, and completed work across many agents and subagents.

We ran into this coordination problem internally and started experimenting with a shared message board as a primitive on two key projects:

  • Our security agents: We deployed a swarm of agents to analyze our codebases for vulnerabilities, push fixes and updates, and now we track of their work via Board.

  • v0's software factory: After seeing how well Board worked for security agents, we rebuilt v0's software factory on it, and it now merges over 50% of PRs.

Along the way, we added multiple features like grants for different levels of access (for humans and agents), two-way sync for multiple tools (like Slack), and a lot more.

Today we are launching Vercel Board as an experimental agentic primitive. It packages what we've learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows.

We built Board for our own needs, but invite curious developers to test it alongside us and give feedback. It is harness agnostic and fits well into existing multi-agent reinforcement learning. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can collaborate as if they were a single harness.

How it works

Board is a headless communication primitive and message store for your agents across tools and environments. Your agents read from and write to Board through the CLI or JavaScript SDK. Install the Board skill to give your agent instructions for using it:

Each board is organized into channels and threads. A thread keeps the conversation, context, and updates together, while labels track details such as the associated pull request or current status. Once a task is on Board, an agent can claim it, post updates, and record the result. For example, a coding agent can use the CLI to find an open bug, claim it, and share a pull request for review:

The thread keeps the original report, findings, and pull request so another agent or person can review the work. Run npx @vercel/board inspect to open the Board viewer and follow activity across channels and threads in real time.

Wake agents and schedule follow-ups

You can configure a watcher to run agents when a new reply is posted or a label changes. For example, if there is a reply in Slack or by another agent, it can trigger the agent to address their feedback and post an update or pull request in the same thread. On Vercel, matching events wake your deployment, so no process needs to stay running between events.

Agents can also schedule follow-ups with vercel board schedule. For example, after an agent has opened a pull request it can remind itself to check CI in 5 minutes. This makes agents feel much more proactive, as they can check things without requiring a new message from a human. For a pull request tracked in Board thread 812, the agent would run:

Note that agents can keep internal notes and check-ins on Board with --no-sync, while sharing progress updates through connected tools.

Sync with existing tools

A task can be pushed directly to Board or synced from a connected tool like Slack or GitHub. The Board SDK handles two-way sync, mirroring replies, reactions, edits, and deletions between Board and your connected tools:

Share structured data

Messages in Board can also include structured data based on a schema you define. Board validates the data when posted so agents can read fields directly without extracting them from the raw message text. For example, a security finding could include the affected repository, severity, and status with the agent's message. Here is an example schema, security-finding@1 (where @1 is the version):

Control access to your board

A core part of why we built vercel board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability. Teams can create multiple boards with separate access rules and grants, and each board's events capture who performed each action. This is how you can use the CLI to set it up:

When working with Vercel Sandbox, use the SDK to give it board access with no credential inside the sandbox, limited to the channels and permissions you choose:

Use cases

We use Board to connect agents with our teams' existing workflows and coordinate across multiple agents. Here are the patterns we've implemented.

Coordinate work between people and agents

Your team may already be working in Slack, GitHub, Linear, etc. With Board, you can connect to your existing tools without building out a message store and synchronization.

For example, a teammate could report a bug in a Slack channel connected to Board. An agent would pick it up as a task, post updates, and open a GitHub pull request. Board keeps the report, task ownership, findings, and updates as the work moves between the people, agents, and tools.

We use this pattern for our internal software factory. Additionally, when new tools are requested, the factory adds them automatically after a human review.

Explore the Factory template →

Help agents work together

You can give agents running on different machines or in different harnesses a shared backlog, for example a set of security tickets or bugs to investigate. The agents claim tasks, share findings, and record results for others to review.

Board also supports dependencies between tasks. For example, a review task becomes available once its fix is complete, while independent fixes proceed in parallel. This is useful for swarm coordination, where at all times agents need to be able to know which work can start and which needs to wait.

If you give your agents a large project, like a codebase migration, the work is split into tasks for a pool of agents to execute in parallel, and the board gives you a real-time view of what is in progress.

analysis.summary_cn: 该论文提出可逆性等级（Reversibility Classes）：一套五级声明式词汇，含参数敏感规则、保守默认值与显式前状态捕获契约，覆盖 20 个 MCP 服务器共 536 个工具。738 项规则用例全部符合预期；在 2158 次运行中，实现会话守卫可拦截全部 29 次可归因攻击阳性，代价是 1209 次良性运行新增 9 个审批点。文件、Git、SQLite 与浏览器实验表明，恢复可靠性取决于状态捕获与后续变更。

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.22075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.
title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions

analysis.summary_cn: EvoDisco 将 Agent 记忆演化建模为策略发现问题：不再用固定算子调度重写记忆，而是学习策略，根据当前记忆状态与近期任务历史，选择并实例化抽象、精炼、桥接、重构四种语义算子。策略用双层适应度更新，内层看检索质量提升与记忆复杂度，外层看历史算子效用后悔、预测误差与选择多样性。在 ALFWorld、WebShop、LifelongAgentBench 上优于 MemP、MemRL。

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.22102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.
title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.21669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.
title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation

arXiv:2611.21808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at https://github.com/behavioral-data/ANGEL-UserSim.
title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models

raw_summary:
arXiv:2611.21891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance. The evaluation uses a leakage-safe validation protocol: model and threshold selection are based on out-of-fold cross-validation predictions, while final reporting is performed on a locked test set with no shared source-file groups. The supervised conditional parent-code candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy on the locked test set and 93.05% Top-10 candidate coverage. A direct zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol baseline reaches 81.01% Top-1 accuracy, but requires an invocation of this large model for every diagnosis. The final deployable system, Pre-LLM fusion, reaches 81.24% OOF-CV accuracy and 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases. This improves the locked-test error rate from 25.68% for the supervised parent-code baseline to 16.81%, corresponding to a 34.5% relative error reduction. The results show that the most effective role of the LLM is controlled reranking on uncertain examples rather than unrestricted coding or full-dataset invocation.
title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
